title: AI Engineer Roadmap for a Novice — Day-by-Day Plan (36 Weeks, 216 Days)

units.title: Set up the machine
units.do: install WSL2 + Ubuntu (Windows) or use Terminal (Mac/Linux). Install VS Code and the "Remote – WSL" extension if on Windows. Open a terminal. Run `whoami`, `pwd`, `ls`, `echo $HOME`.
units.learn: what an operating system is; why developers use Linux/Unix shells.
units.tip: spend the whole hour on setup if needed. A broken environment on Day 1 poisons every day after. Don't skip WSL2 in favour of Windows CMD — every tutorial for the rest of your life assumes a Unix shell.

units.title: Navigate and manipulate files
units.do: `cd`, `ls -la`, `mkdir -p a/b/c`, `touch`, `cp`, `mv`, `rm -r` (carefully), `cat`, `less`, `head`, `tail`. Build a fake project folder tree with 10 files using only the terminal.
units.learn: filesystem tree, absolute vs relative paths, `.` and `..`, hidden files.
units.tip: never run `rm -rf` on a path you didn't just `ls`. Make this a reflex now.

units.title: Search, pipe, redirect
units.do: `grep -r "word" .`, `find . -name "*.txt"`, `wc -l`, `sort | uniq -c`, `history`. Write a one-liner that counts how many lines across all `.txt` files contain a given word.
units.learn: stdin/stdout/stderr; what `|`, `>`, `>>` do.
units.tip: `man command` and `command --help` are your primary documentation. Practise reading them today — it's a skill.

units.title: Git locally
units.do: `git init`, `git status`, `git add`, `git commit -m`, `git log --oneline`, `git diff`. Create `LEARNING_LOG.md` and make 5 commits with meaningful messages. Write a `.gitignore`.
units.learn: what version control is; commit = snapshot; the three areas (working, staged, committed).
units.tip: commit messages in the imperative ("Add log file", not "Added"). Small commits, one idea each. You'll thank yourself in Week 30.

units.title: Git remote and branches
units.do: create a GitHub account (professional username). `git remote add origin`, `git push -u origin main`. `git branch feature`, `git checkout feature` (or `switch`), edit, commit, push, open a pull request on GitHub, merge it, `git pull`.
units.learn: remote vs local; branch = pointer; merge.
units.tip: set up SSH keys today (`ssh-keygen`, add to GitHub). Password prompts on every push will make you avoid pushing.

units.title: Build block: environment + editor mastery
units.do: (1) set up VS Code properly: Python extension, GitLens, auto-save, format-on-save, a dark theme you'll keep. Learn 10 shortcuts: command palette, quick open, multi-cursor, find/replace, toggle terminal, go to line. (2) Learn `nano` and 6 `vim` survival commands (`i`, `Esc`, `:wq`, `:q!`, `dd`, `/search`). (3) Environment variables: `export`, `.bashrc`, `PATH`. (4) Write `README.md` for your repo explaining its purpose. (5) Do a full clean run: delete the local clone, re-clone from GitHub, confirm everything works.
units.tip: the "re-clone" test is the real milestone. If your work only exists on one machine, it doesn't exist.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: DNS, IP, TCP
units.do: `ping`, `nslookup google.com` or `dig`, `curl -I https://example.com`. Write in your log: "when I type a URL and press Enter, the following happens…" (draft 1).
units.learn: what a URL is; DNS resolves names to IPs; TCP carries bytes reliably; ports.
units.tip: you don't need to memorize the OSI model. You need: name → address → connection → request → response.

units.title: HTTP requests and responses
units.do: `curl -v https://httpbin.org/get`, `curl -X POST -d '{"a":1}' -H "Content-Type: application/json" https://httpbin.org/post`. Read every line of the verbose output and annotate it in your log.
units.learn: verbs GET/POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE; status code families 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx; headers; body.
units.tip: `-v` is your best teacher. Most "the API doesn't work" bugs are visible in the verbose headers.

units.title: JSON and public APIs
units.do: pick three free public APIs (a weather API, a public-data API, and one that needs a query parameter). `curl` each. Pipe through `python -m json.tool` to pretty-print. Save responses to files.
units.learn: JSON syntax (objects, arrays, strings, numbers, booleans, null); why APIs use it.
units.tip: read the API docs before calling. Note required headers and rate limits. Half of API integration is reading docs carefully.

units.title: Browser DevTools
units.do: open DevTools → Network tab on three sites. Identify HTML, CSS, JS, XHR/fetch, image requests. Find a JSON API call a website makes and replicate it with `curl`.
units.learn: what the browser does on page load; client vs server; what "frontend" and "backend" mean.
units.tip: this trick — "steal the API call from the Network tab" — will serve you for years in scraping, debugging, and reverse engineering.

units.title: Review and write
units.do: finalize your "URL to page" explanation (1 page, your own words, no copying). Review every command from Weeks 1–2 without notes. Re-do any you can't recall.
units.tip: explaining is the test of understanding. If a sentence feels vague, you don't understand it yet — look it up.

units.title: Build block: Stage 0 exit test
units.do: (1) timed test, 20 min: from a fresh terminal, clone your repo, branch, edit, commit, push, open PR, and `curl` an API with a query parameter and a header. (2) If you fail, spend 2 hours drilling the weak step, then retest. (3) Install Python 3.12+ (via `uv` or python.org) and confirm `python --version`. (4) Read the first chapter of your chosen Python book. (5) Update README with a "Stage 0 complete" section listing what you can now do.
units.tip: passing the timed test without notes is non-negotiable. Everything in Stage 1 assumes it.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Variables and types
units.do: open `python` REPL and experiment for 20 min. Then write `day_01.py`: 10 variables of each type, print them with `f"..."`. Try `"3" + 3` and read the error carefully.
units.learn: int, float, str, bool, None; `type()`; dynamic typing; the REPL.
units.tip: read every error message top to bottom before Googling. The last line tells you the type; the lines above tell you where. This habit is worth more than any tutorial.

units.title: Strings
units.do: 10 string exercises: reverse a string, count vowels, title-case a sentence manually, check if a word is in a sentence, extract a domain from an email.
units.learn: indexing, slicing `s[1:4]`, `.upper() .lower() .strip() .split() .join() .replace() .find()`, `in`, `len()`.
units.tip: strings are immutable — every method returns a new string. `s.upper()` does nothing unless you assign it.

units.title: Conditionals
units.do: FizzBuzz, leap-year checker, grade calculator, BMI category, simple login check. CodeWars 8kyu ×3.
units.learn: `if/elif/else`, comparison operators, `and/or/not`, truthiness (empty string/list/0/None are false).
units.tip: `==` compares, `=` assigns. Also: `if x == True` should just be `if x`.

units.title: Loops
units.do: print a multiplication table, sum of digits, find primes under 100, number guessing game with `while`, draw a triangle of `*`. CodeWars 8kyu ×4.
units.learn: `for x in ...`, `range(start, stop, step)`, `while`, `break`, `continue`, nested loops.
units.tip: off-by-one errors live in `range()`. `range(5)` is 0–4. Print the loop variable when confused.

units.title: Review
units.do: CodeWars 8kyu ×3 (aim for 10 total this week). Re-solve Day 3 and Day 4 problems from memory. Read one Python solution on CodeWars that's shorter than yours and understand why.
units.tip: reading others' solutions after solving is how you learn idioms. Reading before solving is how you learn nothing.

units.title: Build block
units.do: (1) 2 h: book chapters on input/output and basic control flow, typing every example. (2) 3 h: build a terminal "quiz game": asks 10 questions from a hard-coded list, tracks score, allows retry, handles bad input. (3) 1 h: 15 small scripts committed (you should be there by now). (4) 1 h: log what confused you this week.
units.tip: the quiz game will feel too easy or too hard. Either way, finish it. Finishing is the skill.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Lists
units.do: implement: max without `max()`, second largest, remove duplicates, rotate a list, matrix transpose with nested lists. CodeWars 8kyu ×3.
units.learn: creating, indexing (negative too), slicing, `.append() .insert() .pop() .remove() .sort() .reverse()`, `sorted()`, `len`, `in`, list of lists.
units.tip: `.sort()` returns `None` and sorts in place; `sorted()` returns a new list. This bites everyone once.

units.title: Tuples and sets
units.do: deduplicate a list preserving order (hint: seen-set); find common elements of two lists; count unique words in a paragraph. CodeWars 7kyu ×2.
units.learn: tuples are immutable lists (use for fixed records); sets are unordered unique items with fast membership; set operations `| & - ^`.
units.tip: when you need "is X in this collection?" many times, use a set. It's O(1) vs O(n) — you'll learn what that means in Week 5; feel it now by timing both on 100,000 items.

units.title: Dictionaries
units.do: word-frequency counter; invert a dict; group a list of names by first letter; phone-book lookup. CodeWars 7kyu ×2.
units.learn: key/value, `d[key]`, `.get(key, default)`, `.keys() .values() .items()`, adding/updating/deleting, `in`, nested dicts.
units.tip: `d.get(k, 0) + 1` is the counting idiom. Learn `collections.Counter` and `defaultdict` today too — you'll use them weekly.

units.title: Comprehensions and iteration helpers
units.do: rewrite 5 earlier loops as comprehensions; sort a list of (name, age) tuples by age; pair two lists with `zip`; number lines with `enumerate`. CodeWars 7kyu ×3.
units.learn: list/dict/set comprehensions, conditional comprehensions, `enumerate`, `zip`, `sorted(key=...)`, `lambda` (just enough), `min/max(key=...)`.
units.tip: if a comprehension needs more than one `if` or nesting, write a loop. Readability beats cleverness.

units.title: Review
units.do: CodeWars 7kyu ×5. Re-implement Counter, defaultdict-grouping, and dedup-preserving-order from memory. Time yourself.
units.tip: you should now be able to read a 7kyu problem and know which data structure fits within 30 seconds. If not, do 5 more.

units.title: Build block: Contact Book v1
units.do: a CLI contact book. Menu loop: add, list, search (by partial name), delete, quit. Contacts stored as a list of dicts. Validate input (no empty names, phone must be digits). Search is case-insensitive. Commit in stages: menu → add/list → search → delete → validation.
units.tip: write the menu loop first with all options printing "not implemented". Then fill one at a time. This is how professionals build: skeleton, then flesh.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Functions
units.do: convert every Week 3–4 script into functions. Write `is_palindrome`, `flatten`, `chunk(lst, n)`, `most_common(lst)`. CodeWars 7kyu ×2.
units.learn: `def`, parameters vs arguments, `return` (vs print), default values, keyword arguments, docstrings, scope (local vs global).
units.tip: a function that prints instead of returning can't be tested or reused. Return values; print at the edges.

units.title: `*args`, `**kwargs`, type hints
units.do: add type hints to every function from Day 1. Install `mypy` and run it — fix what it reports. Write a `sum_all(*numbers)` and `make_profile(**fields)`.
units.learn: variable arguments; type hints `def f(x: int, names: list[str]) -> dict[str, int]`; why hints matter (editor help, catching bugs, documentation).
units.tip: type hints are not enforced at runtime. They're for you, your editor, and your future teammates. Use them everywhere from today; it will make Pydantic in Stage 3 feel natural.

units.title: Modules and the standard library
units.do: split your utility functions into `utils.py` and import them from `main.py`. Write a script using `pathlib` to list all `.py` files in your repo with their sizes. Use `datetime` to compute days until a date.
units.learn: `import`, `from x import y`, `if __name__ == "__main__":`, creating your own module; tour of `math`, `random`, `datetime`, `os`, `pathlib`, `json`, `collections`, `itertools`.
units.tip: `pathlib.Path` over `os.path` — always. It's cleaner and cross-platform.

units.title: Virtual environments and pip
units.do: create a venv for `python-practice`, install `requests` and `rich`, freeze requirements, add `.venv/` to `.gitignore`. Delete the venv and recreate it from `requirements.txt`.
units.learn: why isolation matters (project A needs version 1, project B needs version 2); `python -m venv .venv`, activate, `pip install`, `pip freeze > requirements.txt`; or `uv` as a faster alternative.
units.tip: never `pip install` outside a venv again. If your prompt doesn't show `(.venv)`, stop.

units.title: Review
units.do: CodeWars 7kyu ×5. Write, from memory, a module with 5 typed, documented functions and a `__main__` block that demos them. Run `mypy` clean.
units.tip: if `mypy` complains about something you think is fine, you've found a gap in your mental model. Chase it.

units.title: Build block: Contact Book v2
units.do: refactor Contact Book into a package: `contacts/models.py` (functions that create/validate a contact), `contacts/store.py` (add/search/delete), `contacts/cli.py` (menu), `main.py`. Full type hints, docstrings, `mypy` clean, inside a venv with `requirements.txt`. Add a `--help` using `argparse`.
units.tip: the refactor will feel like wasted time. It isn't — you're learning to move code without breaking it, which is 60% of real engineering.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Reading and writing files
units.do: write a script that reads a text file and reports line/word/character counts; append a timestamp to a log file each run; copy a file line by line.
units.learn: `open()`, modes `r/w/a`, `with` (context managers close files), reading lines, writing lines, encodings (`utf-8`).
units.tip: always `with open(...)`. Forgetting to close files causes data loss you won't notice until it matters.

units.title: CSV and JSON
units.do: create a CSV of 20 fake contacts by hand; read it with `DictReader`; convert to JSON; read JSON back; compare. Download a real CSV dataset and load it.
units.learn: `csv.reader/writer/DictReader/DictWriter`; `json.load/loads/dump/dumps`; `indent=2`; what round-tripping means.
units.tip: CSVs from the real world are dirty — extra spaces, missing fields, mixed encodings. Assume nothing; `.strip()` everything.

units.title: Exceptions
units.do: make yesterday's CSV loader survive: missing file, empty file, malformed rows, missing columns. Each failure gets a clear message. Write a `parse_int(s)` that returns `None` on failure.
units.learn: `try/except/else/finally`; catching specific exceptions (`ValueError`, `FileNotFoundError`, `KeyError`, `ZeroDivisionError`); `raise`; custom exceptions via `class MyError(Exception)`; never bare `except:`.
units.tip: catch the narrowest exception you can, as close to the source as you can. `except Exception:` hides bugs.

units.title: Logging
units.do: replace every diagnostic `print` in your projects with `logging`. Log to both console and `app.log`. Log exceptions with `logger.exception()`.
units.learn: `logging` module: levels DEBUG/INFO/WARNING/ERROR, `basicConfig`, format strings, logging to a file, why not `print()` for diagnostics.
units.tip: `logger.exception()` inside an `except` block captures the traceback automatically. Use it.

units.title: Review
units.do: CodeWars 7kyu ×5. Build a "messy CSV to clean JSON report" script from a spec you write yourself: handles at least 5 failure modes, logs each, never crashes.
units.tip: deliberately corrupt your input files in 5 different ways and confirm each is handled. Testing your own error handling is a professional habit.

units.title: Build block: Contact Book v3
units.do: contacts persist to `contacts.json`; load on start, save on every change. Survive missing/corrupt file (back it up and start fresh, with a warning). Add import-from-CSV and export-to-CSV commands. Logging throughout. Custom `ContactNotFound` exception. Commit each feature.
units.tip: write the "corrupt file" case first. Happy paths are easy; robustness is what employers pay for.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Classes and instances
units.do: `Contact` class with name/phone/email and `is_valid()`; `BankAccount` with deposit/withdraw that raises on overdraft; `Rectangle` with area/perimeter. CodeWars 7kyu ×2.
units.learn: `class`, `__init__`, `self`, attributes, methods, `__repr__`/`__str__`. A class bundles data with behaviour.
units.tip: `self` is just the instance. If you get "missing 1 required positional argument: self", you called a method on the class instead of an instance.

units.title: Dataclasses and properties
units.do: rewrite Day 1 classes as dataclasses. Add a `full_name` property. Try mutating a frozen dataclass and read the error.
units.learn: `@dataclass` generates `__init__`, `__repr__`, `__eq__`; `field(default_factory=list)`; `frozen=True`; `@property` for computed attributes.
units.tip: dataclasses for data, regular classes for behaviour-heavy objects. Default to dataclass — it's what Pydantic builds on in Stage 3.

units.title: Inheritance and composition
units.do: `Shape` → `Circle`, `Square` with `area()`; then a `Library` that *has* a list of `Book` and `Member` objects (composition). Model a `Loan` linking them. CodeWars 6kyu ×1.
units.learn: `class Dog(Animal)`, `super().__init__()`, method overriding; composition ("has a") vs inheritance ("is a"); why composition is usually better.
units.tip: if you're more than two levels deep in inheritance, stop and use composition. Deep hierarchies are a classic beginner trap.

units.title: When NOT to use classes; dunder methods
units.do: make `Library` iterable and support `len()`. Add `Contact.from_dict()` classmethod and `to_dict()`. Sort a list of contacts by name using `__lt__`.
units.learn: functions and dicts are often enough; `__len__`, `__iter__`, `__getitem__`, `__eq__`, `__lt__` for sorting; `@classmethod` and `@staticmethod`.
units.tip: don't wrap two functions in a class just to feel "object-oriented". Classes earn their place when state and behaviour genuinely belong together.

units.title: Review
units.do: CodeWars 6kyu ×3. Write the library system (Book, Member, Loan) from memory with dataclasses, a `Library` class managing them, and a `__main__` demo.
units.tip: draw the relationships on paper before coding. Five minutes of boxes and arrows saves an hour of refactoring.

units.title: Build block: Contact Book v4
units.do: `Contact` dataclass; `Storage` class with `load()/save()/add()/find()/delete()` wrapping the JSON file; `ContactBook` class using `Storage` (composition); CLI calls `ContactBook`. `from_dict/to_dict` for serialization. Sorting and iteration supported. Everything typed and `mypy` clean.
units.tip: the `Storage` abstraction is deliberate — in Week 10 you'll swap JSON for SQLite by changing one class. That's what good design buys you.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: pytest basics
units.do: write tests for all Week 5 utility functions (`is_palindrome`, `flatten`, `chunk`, `most_common`). Include edge cases: empty input, single element, wrong type.
units.learn: install `pytest`; test files `test_*.py`; functions `test_*`; `assert`; running `pytest -v`; reading failure output.
units.tip: one assertion idea per test; name tests by behaviour (`test_flatten_handles_empty_list`). A failing test should tell you what broke without reading the code.

units.title: Fixtures, parametrize, coverage
units.do: parametrize your palindrome tests with 10 cases; test that `BankAccount.withdraw` raises on overdraft; test `Storage` using `tmp_path` so real files aren't touched. Reach 100% coverage on `utils.py`.
units.learn: `@pytest.fixture` for setup; `@pytest.mark.parametrize` for many inputs; `pytest.raises`; `pytest-cov` and reading a coverage report; `tmp_path` fixture for file tests.
units.tip: 100% coverage doesn't mean bug-free; it means every line ran. Still, aim for it on small modules — it forces you to think about edge cases.

units.title: Test-first
units.do: build a `PhoneNumber` normalizer test-first: accepts `+92 300 1234567`, `0300-1234567`, `(0300) 1234567`, rejects letters. Write each test before the code that satisfies it.
units.learn: TDD loop: write failing test → minimal code to pass → refactor.
units.tip: TDD feels slow the first day and fast forever after. Push through today.

units.title: HTTP with `requests`
units.do: call the three public APIs from Week 2 from Python. Handle 404, timeout, and bad JSON. Write a `fetch_json(url, params) -> dict | None` helper with retries (3 attempts, sleep between).
units.learn: `requests.get/post`, `params=`, `headers=`, `json=`, `.status_code`, `.json()`, `.raise_for_status()`, `timeout=` (always), sessions.
units.tip: always pass `timeout=`. Without it a hung server hangs your program forever. This is a real production incident waiting to happen.

units.title: Mocking the network
units.do: write tests for `fetch_json` that mock success, 404, timeout, and malformed JSON. CodeWars 6kyu ×2.
units.learn: why tests shouldn't hit real networks (slow, flaky, costs money); `unittest.mock.patch`, `responses` library or `pytest-httpx`.
units.tip: mock at the boundary (the `requests.get` call), not deep inside your code. Over-mocking makes tests meaningless.

units.title: Build block: API client + full test suite
units.do: (1) 3 h: `api_client/` project — a CLI that fetches from a public API, caches results in a local JSON with a timestamp (skip the network if cache < 1 hour old), and prints a formatted summary using `rich`. (2) 3 h: full test suite for Contact Book v4 (Storage, ContactBook, validation) with `tmp_path`, plus mocked tests for the API client. (3) 1 h: add a `Makefile` or `justfile` with `test`, `lint`, `run` targets; add `ruff` for linting.
units.tip: run `pytest` before every commit from now until forever. Add it to your Friday review ritual.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Spec
units.do: write a one-page spec for your capstone CLI: "fetch data from [chosen public API], clean it, store as JSON and CSV, produce a summary report with statistics and a top-N list." Define inputs, outputs, error cases, and what "done" means. Draw the module layout.
units.tip: choose an API with imperfect data (public datasets, not toy endpoints). Dirty data teaches more than clean data.

units.title: Fetch layer
units.do: `fetcher.py` with typed functions, timeouts, retries, caching, logging. Tests with mocked network. Commit.
units.tip: build and test one layer per day. Vertical slices, not horizontal sprawl.

units.title: Clean and model layer
units.do: `models.py` with dataclasses for your records including `from_api(dict)` that validates and normalizes; `cleaner.py` that drops/repairs bad rows and logs each decision. Tests with 10 malformed inputs.
units.tip: log *why* each row was dropped. In Stage 3 you'll do exactly this for LLM outputs.

units.title: Storage and report layer
units.do: `storage.py` writes JSON and CSV; `report.py` computes stats (count, mean, min/max, top-N by a field) and renders a table with `rich`. Tests for stats on known data.
units.tip: compute statistics on a tiny hand-checked dataset in your tests. If `mean([1,2,3])` isn't 2, everything downstream is wrong.

units.title: CLI, README, polish
units.do: `argparse` CLI with subcommands `fetch`, `report`, `export`. README with install/run instructions and a screenshot. `ruff` clean, `mypy` clean, `pytest` green. CodeWars 6kyu ×3.
units.tip: the README is for a stranger. Have someone (or your future self after a week) follow it from scratch.

units.title: Build block: Stage 1 exit test
units.do: (1) 2 h timed, no AI, no notes: implement from an unseen spec — "parse a web-server log file (write a generator script first to create 10,000 fake lines), report top 5 error types per hour, output JSON and a table." Must be typed, modular, tested. (2) Grade yourself honestly against the spec. (3) If failed: identify the weak area (structure? testing? parsing?), spend 3 hours drilling it, retest next weekend before starting Stage 2. (4) If passed: 2 h reading SQLBolt intro and installing SQLite tooling; 1 h retrospective in your log — what was hardest in Stage 1 and why.
units.tip: most people fail this on structure and tests, not on Python syntax. That's the point of the test.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Tables and SELECT
units.do: SQLBolt lessons 1–4. In `sqlite3`, create a `contacts` table and insert 10 rows by hand; run 10 different SELECTs.
units.learn: relational model — table, row, column, type; `CREATE TABLE`, `INSERT`, `SELECT ... FROM ... WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, `DISTINCT`.
units.tip: SQL is declarative — you say *what* you want, not *how*. Novices try to "loop" in SQL. Think in sets of rows.

units.title: Filtering and functions
units.do: SQLBolt 5–8. Write 15 queries against your contacts table using every operator above.
units.learn: `LIKE`, `IN`, `BETWEEN`, `IS NULL`, `AND/OR/NOT`, string functions, `CASE WHEN`, `COALESCE`.
units.tip: `NULL` is not equal to anything, including `NULL`. Use `IS NULL`. This causes silent wrong answers, not errors.

units.title: Aggregation
units.do: SQLBolt 9–12. Load a real CSV into SQLite (`.import`), then: rows per category, average per group, groups with more than N rows, top 5 by a metric.
units.learn: `COUNT SUM AVG MIN MAX`, `GROUP BY`, `HAVING` (filter after grouping) vs `WHERE` (filter before).
units.tip: every non-aggregated column in `SELECT` must be in `GROUP BY`. SQLite is lenient about this; Postgres will reject it. Write it correctly now.

units.title: SQLite from Python
units.do: script that creates the contacts table, inserts from your Week 6 CSV, and runs 5 queries. Then deliberately try string-formatting a query with user input and inject `'; DROP TABLE contacts; --` — watch it work. Then fix with parameters.
units.learn: `sqlite3.connect`, cursor, `execute`, `executemany`, `fetchall/fetchone`, parameterized queries with `?`, `commit`, `with conn:`.
units.tip: you just performed SQL injection on yourself. Never build a query with f-strings or `+`. Parameters, always. This is interview material.

units.title: Review
units.do: SQLBolt remaining lessons. From memory, write: a table with 3 constraints, 5 SELECTs covering filter/sort/aggregate, and a parameterized Python insert.
units.tip: read `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` output for one query today just to see it exists. You'll use it seriously on Day 3 of Week 11.

units.title: Build block: Contact Book v5 on SQLite
units.do: replace the JSON `Storage` class with a `SqliteStorage` class implementing the same methods — the rest of the app should not change. Schema with constraints (`NOT NULL`, `UNIQUE` on email). Migrations as numbered SQL files applied on startup. Tests using an in-memory database (`:memory:`). Import/export still work.
units.tip: if you have to change `ContactBook` or the CLI to swap storage, your Week 7 abstraction leaked. Fix the abstraction, not the callers.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Keys and relationships
units.do: design on paper, then create: `patients`, `doctors`, `appointments` (FK to both), `prescriptions` (FK to appointment). Insert 5 of each. Delete a patient and observe cascade.
units.learn: primary key, foreign key, one-to-many, many-to-many via junction table; `REFERENCES`; `ON DELETE CASCADE`.
units.tip: many-to-many always needs a third table. If you find yourself storing comma-separated IDs in a column, stop — that's the classic beginner schema error.

units.title: Joins
units.do: pgexercises "Joins and Subqueries" section (do it on SQLite or set up Postgres early). On your clinic schema: appointments with patient and doctor names; doctors with zero appointments (LEFT JOIN + IS NULL); prescriptions with all four tables joined.
units.learn: `INNER JOIN`, `LEFT JOIN`, (`RIGHT`, `FULL` rarely), join conditions, table aliases, joining three tables, self-join.
units.tip: draw the Venn diagram for each join type once, then never again — instead, ask "which table's rows must all appear?" That table goes on the LEFT.

units.title: Subqueries and indexes
units.do: generate 100,000 fake appointments with a Python script. Time a query filtering by `doctor_id` before and after `CREATE INDEX`. Read the plan for both. Rewrite one nested subquery as a CTE.
units.learn: subqueries in `WHERE` and `FROM`, `EXISTS`, CTEs (`WITH ... AS`); what an index is (a sorted lookup structure), `CREATE INDEX`, when it helps (filter/join columns), when it hurts (write-heavy tables); `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN`.
units.tip: the 100k-row timing demo is the single most important thing this week. Feel the difference; don't just read about it.

units.title: Normalization, just enough
units.do: take a deliberately bad flat table (patient name, doctor name, doctor phone, appointment date, drug all in one row) and normalize it into your clinic schema. Write the migration.
units.learn: 1NF (atomic values), 2NF/3NF (no partial or transitive dependencies) in plain terms: "don't repeat facts; store each fact once and reference it." When denormalization is acceptable (read-heavy reporting).
units.tip: the smell of bad design is *update anomalies* — changing a doctor's phone in 400 rows. If updating one fact means touching many rows, normalize.

units.title: Review
units.do: pgexercises "Aggregates" section. From memory: create the clinic schema with constraints and two indexes, write 10 queries including a 3-table join, a LEFT JOIN with NULL check, a CTE, and a `GROUP BY` with `HAVING`.
units.tip: the 10 queries should read like questions a clinic manager would ask. If you can't phrase the business question, you don't need the query.

units.title: Build block: transactions and a reporting script
units.do: (3 h) Python script that books an appointment transactionally: check doctor availability, insert appointment, insert prescription placeholder — all-or-nothing; simulate a failure mid-way and confirm rollback. (3 h) reporting script: appointments per doctor per month, top drugs prescribed, patients with no visits in 6 months — output as a `rich` table. Tests on a seeded `:memory:` DB.
units.learn: (1 h): transactions — `BEGIN/COMMIT/ROLLBACK`, atomicity, why a transfer between two accounts must be one transaction; isolation in one paragraph.
units.tip: the "simulate failure mid-transaction" test is the one interviewers ask about. Make sure you can explain why the rollback happened.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Install and explore Postgres
units.do: install locally (native or `docker run postgres` — preview of Week 23; the one-liner is fine to copy today). Connect with `psql`. Learn `\l \c \dt \d table \q \x`. Create a database, a user, grant privileges.
units.learn: Postgres vs SQLite — a server process, users/roles, databases, schemas; why it's the industry default (concurrency, extensions, reliability).
units.tip: Postgres setup frustration is universal. Budget the whole hour; if you finish early, explore `\?` for psql commands.

units.title: Port the schema
units.do: port the clinic schema to Postgres with proper types and constraints. Insert with `RETURNING id`. Try `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` for an upsert. Run yesterday's 10 queries and fix what Postgres rejects that SQLite allowed.
units.learn: Postgres types (`SERIAL`/`GENERATED AS IDENTITY`, `TEXT`, `TIMESTAMPTZ`, `NUMERIC`, `BOOLEAN`, `JSONB`), `RETURNING`, `ON CONFLICT`.
units.tip: use `TIMESTAMPTZ`, never `TIMESTAMP`. Timezone bugs are miserable and permanent.

units.title: Python with psycopg
units.do: rewrite the transactional booking script and the reporting script against Postgres. Credentials via `.env` loaded with `python-dotenv`. `.env` in `.gitignore`.
units.learn: `psycopg` (v3): `connect`, `cursor`, `execute` with `%s` parameters, `fetchall`, `commit`, context managers, connection strings, reading credentials from environment variables, `dict_row` row factory.
units.tip: never commit a `.env`. Add a `.env.example` with placeholder values instead. Leaked database credentials in public repos get scanned and exploited within minutes.

units.title: Seeding and timing at scale
units.do: seed 1,000 patients, 100 doctors, 200,000 appointments with `Faker`. Run 5 queries with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`; add indexes on foreign keys and the date column; re-run and record before/after in your log.
units.learn: `executemany` vs `COPY` for bulk loads; `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` in Postgres (actual timings); sequential scan vs index scan.
units.tip: Postgres does not automatically index foreign keys. Many real-world slow queries are exactly this omission.

units.title: Review
units.do: pgexercises "Modifying data" and "String" sections. Write a `db.py` module with a `get_connection()` helper, a `run_query(sql, params)` helper, and tests against a test database (create/drop in a fixture).
units.tip: separate "connect" from "query" from "business logic." This three-layer split reappears in FastAPI in Week 22.

units.title: Build block: migrations and a data layer
units.do: (4 h) build a `migrate.py` that applies unapplied `migrations/NNN_*.sql` files in order and records them; write 4 migrations evolving the clinic schema (add a column, add an index, add a table, backfill data). (2 h) refactor the reporting script to use the `db.py` layer; add 3 more reports. Tests green.
units.learn: (1 h): what migrations are and why teams need them; Alembic in concept (you'll use it in Week 22); for now, numbered SQL files with a `schema_migrations` table.
units.tip: migrations must be forward-only and idempotent. Run `migrate.py` twice; the second run must do nothing.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: pandas basics
units.do: load a real public dataset (few thousand rows). Answer 10 questions about it using pandas only. Compare with the same questions in SQL — note which feels natural where.
units.learn: `DataFrame`, `read_csv`, `.head() .info() .describe()`, selecting columns, boolean filtering, `.loc/.iloc`, sorting, `.value_counts()`.
units.tip: pandas and SQL overlap heavily. Rule of thumb: filtering/joining large data → SQL; analysis/transformation of a result → pandas.

units.title: groupby, merge, and SQL interop
units.do: read the clinic tables from Postgres into DataFrames; reproduce three of your SQL reports in pandas; write a cleaned DataFrame back to a new table.
units.learn: `.groupby().agg()`, `.merge()` (it's a join), `.pivot_table()`, `pd.read_sql`, `.to_sql`, handling missing values (`.isna() .fillna() .dropna()`).
units.tip: `merge` default is inner join. Same LEFT/INNER reasoning as Week 11 applies.

units.title: Just enough maths: vectors
units.do: with `numpy`: implement `dot`, `norm`, `cosine_similarity` by hand; verify against `numpy.dot` and `numpy.linalg.norm`. Compute pairwise similarity for 5 hand-made vectors and rank them. Implement `top_k(query_vec, matrix, k)`.
units.learn: a vector is a list of numbers; dot product; vector length (norm); cosine similarity = dot / (norm × norm) → 1 means "same direction", 0 unrelated, −1 opposite. Why this measures similarity of meaning in Stage 3.
units.tip: you are writing the core of every vector search engine today. Keep this file — you'll reuse it in Week 17.

units.title: Just enough maths: statistics and probability
units.do: compute all of these on your dataset with numpy/pandas. Build a tiny classifier by rule (e.g. "flag appointments longer than 60 min") and compute its precision/recall against a hand-labelled sample of 50.
units.learn: mean, median, variance, standard deviation, percentiles (p50/p95 — you'll see these in monitoring); what a probability distribution is; why "temperature" in LLMs is about sampling from a distribution; precision, recall, accuracy with a 2×2 table.
units.tip: precision and recall will be your daily language from Week 18. Learn them on 50 rows you can count by hand.

units.title: Plotting and review
units.do: two charts from your dataset. Then, from memory: cosine similarity + top_k, a groupby report, and precision/recall from a confusion matrix.
units.learn: `matplotlib` basics: bar, line, histogram, labels, titles, saving to PNG. Seaborn optional.
units.tip: every chart needs a title, axis labels, and units. Unlabelled charts are the data-analysis equivalent of untyped functions.

units.title: Build block: Stage 2 exit test + data report
units.do: (1) 2 h timed exit test: from a written description of a small business ("a gym with members, classes, trainers, bookings, payments"), design the schema with constraints and two justified indexes, load 50 fake rows per table into Postgres via Python, write 5 queries including a 3-table join, and read the `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` for the join out loud. (2) 4 h: a `report/` project — load a public dataset into Postgres, analyze with pandas, produce a markdown report with two charts and five findings, committed with the code that generated it. (3) 1 h: retrospective; read the first section of a provider's LLM API docs.
units.tip: the "read the query plan aloud" part is deliberate. If you can explain a seq scan vs index scan to a rubber duck, you've passed.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Tokens
units.do: use a tokenizer to count tokens for 10 texts — English prose, code, Urdu/Arabic script, numbers, JSON. Record the words-to-tokens ratio for each in your log.
units.learn: an LLM predicts the next token; a token is a chunk of text (roughly ¾ of a word in English, worse for other languages and code); tokenizers; you pay per token in and out.
units.tip: non-English text and JSON with lots of punctuation are token-expensive. This affects cost and context budgeting later — notice it now.

units.title: First API call
units.do: make one call from Python. Print the response text and the token usage. Compute the cost from the provider's price table. Wrap it in `ask(prompt: str) -> str` with error handling and a timeout.
units.learn: messages format (system, user, assistant), the request/response shape, `max_tokens`, reading usage from the response.
units.tip: print `usage` on every call for the rest of this stage. Cost awareness is a professional reflex, and interviewers ask about it.

units.title: Sampling and context
units.do: same prompt at temperature 0, 0.7, 1.2 — five runs each; note variance. Send a prompt that exceeds the context window and read the error. Measure latency vs output length.
units.learn: temperature (0 = deterministic-ish, higher = more random), `top_p`, context window limits, what happens when you exceed it, why long contexts cost more and can degrade quality.
units.tip: use temperature 0 for anything you need to test or evaluate. Randomness makes bugs unreproducible.

units.title: Why models hallucinate
units.do: ask the model 10 factual questions in a niche domain you know well. Verify each answer. Record the hallucination rate. Then repeat with the correct facts pasted into the prompt; record again.
units.learn: the model generates plausible continuations, not verified facts; it has no database; it's confident by construction. Grounding (giving it the facts in the prompt) is the fix — this is the entire motivation for RAG.
units.tip: keep this experiment's results. It's the clearest "why RAG exists" demonstration you'll ever have, and a great interview story.

units.title: Review + chat loop
units.do: build a terminal chat loop that keeps conversation history (a list of messages), shows cumulative token usage and cost, and lets you `/reset`. Handle rate-limit errors with a retry. CodeWars 6kyu ×2 (keep the problem-solving muscle alive).
units.tip: notice that the full history is re-sent every turn — cost grows with conversation length. That's why production systems summarize or truncate history.

units.title: Build block: model comparison harness
units.do: (1) 3 h: a script that runs a set of 20 prompts against two models (e.g. a small and a large one), recording latency, tokens, cost, and output for each into a CSV. (2) 2 h: analyze with pandas — cost per model, p50/p95 latency, output length distribution; two charts. (3) 2 h: read your provider's docs on structured outputs and tool use ahead of next week; write a one-page summary in your log.
units.tip: p95 latency, not average, is what users feel. You learned percentiles in Week 13 — this is where they start mattering.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Prompting that works
units.do: take a bad prompt ("summarize this") and iterate it 5 times on the same 3 documents, recording output quality each time. Write down which change helped most.
units.learn: the handful of patterns that reliably matter: clear task statement, role/context in the system prompt, explicit output format, delimiters around input data (`<document>...</document>`), few-shot examples, "if unsure say so". Ignore "magic phrase" prompt hacks.
units.tip: put the data at the end and the instructions at the top or bottom, never buried in the middle. Test rather than trust folklore.

units.title: Pydantic v2 fundamentals
units.do: define `Receipt(merchant: str, date: date, total: float, items: list[Item])`. Validate 10 hand-written dicts, 3 of them wrong. Print the JSON schema and read it — this schema is what you'll hand to the model.
units.learn: `BaseModel`, field types, `Field(description=..., ge=0)`, validators, `.model_validate()`, `.model_dump()`, `.model_json_schema()`, `ValidationError`.
units.tip: Pydantic is dataclasses with validation. You did the groundwork in Week 7. Everything in FastAPI (Stage 4) is Pydantic.

units.title: Getting JSON from the model
units.do: extract `Receipt` from 10 messy receipt texts using the schema. Parse with `Receipt.model_validate_json`. Count successes. Then try *without* structured mode and count again.
units.learn: structured output / JSON mode in your provider's API; passing a JSON schema; why free-text JSON extraction breaks (markdown fences, trailing commas, commentary).
units.tip: never regex JSON out of prose. Use the schema-enforced mode. When it's unavailable, validate and retry with the error message fed back to the model.

units.title: Validate, retry, measure
units.do: write `extract[T](text, model_class, max_retries=2) -> T | None`. Run it on 50 messy inputs (generate them: receipts, emails, short bios). Record success rate, average retries, cost.
units.learn: the extract → validate → on failure retry with feedback loop; bounded retries; logging every attempt.
units.tip: generic typed functions like this are reusable across every project. Keep a `llm_utils.py` and grow it for the rest of the roadmap.

units.title: Review
units.do: from memory: a Pydantic model with a validator, a structured-output call, and the retry loop. Then measure: does adding one few-shot example to the prompt raise the 50-input success rate? Record the number.
units.tip: every prompt change from now on gets a number attached. "It seems better" is not evidence.

units.title: Build block: extraction pipeline
units.do: (1) 4 h: `extractor/` — reads a folder of unstructured text files, extracts a chosen schema from each with retries, writes results to Postgres (reuse Week 12 skills) and a CSV, logs failures with reasons, and prints a scorecard (success %, cost, p95 latency). (2) 2 h: tests with mocked LLM responses (mock at the SDK call boundary, like Week 8). (3) 1 h: README with the scorecard.
units.tip: mocking the LLM in tests is essential — real calls are slow, cost money, and are non-deterministic. Your tests must run offline.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Tool calling concept
units.do: define one tool `get_weather(city)` (stub returning fake data). Send a question; inspect the raw response to see the tool-call block; execute it; send the result back; print the final answer.
units.learn: you describe tools (name, description, JSON schema of parameters); the model decides whether to call one and returns structured arguments; *your code* executes it; you send the result back; the model continues.
units.tip: the model never runs code. It only *asks*. Everything dangerous happens in your executor — that's where validation and permissions live.

units.title: Multiple tools and the loop
units.do: three tools — `get_weather`, `calculate(expression)` (use a safe evaluator, never `eval`), `lookup_contact(name)` reading your Postgres contacts. Build the loop. Ask compound questions ("what's the weather where Ahmed lives?").
units.learn: a tool registry (dict name → function + schema); the agent loop: call model → if tool call, execute and append result → repeat until a final text answer; max-iteration guard.
units.tip: always cap iterations (e.g. 10). An uncapped loop with a confused model is a runaway bill.

units.title: Tool schemas from Pydantic
units.do: refactor tools so each has a Pydantic args model; generate schemas automatically; validate arguments and return a structured error to the model if invalid. Watch the model self-correct.
units.learn: generating tool parameter schemas from Pydantic models; good descriptions matter more than clever prompts; validating tool arguments before execution.
units.tip: tool descriptions are prompts. Write them as instructions to a smart intern: what it does, when to use it, what it returns.

units.title: Evaluating tool choice
units.do: write 20 test questions with the expected tool (or "none"). Run the agent at temperature 0; log chosen tool and args; compute accuracy. Improve the worst tool description; re-run; record the delta.
units.learn: for agents, "did it pick the right tool with the right arguments?" is a measurable eval.
units.tip: this is your first agent eval. The pattern — labelled expectations, automated run, a single number, iterate — is the same pattern for every eval you'll ever build.

units.title: Review
units.do: rebuild the tool loop from memory in 45 minutes. Add a `--verbose` flag that prints every model/tool exchange. CodeWars 6kyu ×2.
units.tip: verbose tracing of every step is the primitive version of what Langfuse does in Week 26. Build the habit now.

units.title: Build block: database-aware assistant
units.do: (1) 4 h: an agent over your clinic Postgres DB with tools: `list_tables`, `describe_table`, `run_read_only_query(sql)` (enforce SELECT-only, add LIMIT, timeout), `book_appointment(...)` (validated, transactional — Week 11). Natural-language questions become answers with the SQL shown. (2) 2 h: 20-question eval set with expected answers; report accuracy. (3) 1 h: write a threat-model paragraph: what could go wrong if the query tool weren't read-only? (Preview of Week 27.)
units.tip: the read-only enforcement must be in *code* (parse/allow-list), not in the prompt. Prompts are suggestions; code is a boundary.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: What embeddings are
units.do: embed 10 sentences (some paraphrases, some unrelated) via the API. Compute all pairwise cosine similarities with your Week 13 code. Rank and eyeball — do paraphrases cluster?
units.learn: an embedding turns text into a vector so that similar meanings are close (high cosine similarity). Embedding models are separate from chat models. Dimensions (e.g. 1024–3072). They're the bridge between "search" and "meaning".
units.tip: same model for indexing and querying, always. Mixing embedding models gives garbage similarities with no error.

units.title: Chunking
units.do: pick a document set you care about (a textbook chapter, docs, policies — 50–200 pages). Write `chunk(text, size, overlap) -> list[Chunk]` with a `Chunk` dataclass (id, text, source, index). Produce chunks at 300, 600, 1200 characters; inspect samples of each.
units.learn: documents are too long to embed whole; you split into chunks; strategies: fixed characters, by sentence/paragraph, with overlap; chunk size trades precision against context; store metadata (source, position) with every chunk.
units.tip: chunk on natural boundaries (paragraphs) where possible. Splitting mid-sentence hurts retrieval more than any embedding-model choice.

units.title: Build the index
units.do: embed all chunks (600-char version), persist the matrix and metadata, write `load_index()`. Record total cost and time.
units.learn: batching embedding calls; storing vectors as a numpy matrix plus a parallel list of chunks; persisting with `np.save` and JSON; embedding cost estimation.
units.tip: cache embeddings keyed by a hash of the chunk text. Re-embedding unchanged text on every run wastes money and time.

units.title: Retrieval
units.do: `retrieve(question, k=5) -> list[ScoredChunk]`. Try 10 questions; print the top-5 chunks and scores. Note where the right chunk ranks.
units.learn: query embedding → cosine against the matrix → top-k; returning chunks with scores; the `k` trade-off.
units.tip: print scores. A top-1 at 0.45 and a top-1 at 0.85 mean very different things. You'll use score thresholds in Week 27 to refuse when nothing relevant exists.

units.title: Manual recall@5
units.do: write 20 questions; for each, identify the correct chunk(s) by reading the source. Run retrieval; mark hits by hand. Compute recall@5 and recall@1. This is the seed of your golden set.
units.learn: recall@k = fraction of questions where a correct chunk appears in the top k. It's the core retrieval metric.
units.tip: label by hand today even though it's tedious. Evals built on labels you didn't verify are worthless.

units.title: Build block: retrieval experiments
units.do: (1) 2 h: grow the golden set to 30 questions with labelled correct chunk IDs, stored as JSON. (2) 2 h: `eval_retrieval.py` that computes recall@1/@5 automatically from the golden set. (3) 3 h: run the eval across chunk sizes 300/600/1200 and overlap 0/100; tabulate results; pick the best and write a paragraph explaining why.
units.tip: you've just run your first controlled experiment on an AI system. One variable at a time, one number, a decision. That's the job.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Assemble RAG
units.do: `answer(question) -> Answer(text, sources)` using a Pydantic model. Instruct the model to cite chunk IDs and to say "not found in the documents" when the context doesn't contain the answer. Test on your 30 questions.
units.learn: the pipeline: question → retrieve top-k → build a prompt with the chunks as context (with source IDs) → generate → return answer plus citations.
units.tip: "answer only from the provided context; if absent, say so" is the single most important line in a RAG prompt. Without it you've built a hallucination machine with extra steps.

units.title: Golden set with answers
units.do: add a reference answer to each of the 30 questions (hand-written from the source). Add 5 "unanswerable" questions where the correct behaviour is refusal.
units.learn: a golden set pairs questions with correct chunks *and* reference answers; evaluation compares generated answers to references.
units.tip: include unanswerable questions from day one. A system that never says "I don't know" will fail in production on exactly the questions that matter.

units.title: Answer evaluation
units.do: implement `judge(question, reference, generated) -> Grade` with structured output. Run on all 35. Report answer accuracy, refusal accuracy on the 5 unanswerables, retrieval recall@5, cost, p95 latency — one scorecard.
units.learn: exact match (rare), substring/keyword match (crude), LLM-as-judge (a second model call grading the answer against the reference on a rubric — correct/partial/wrong); judge prompts must be strict and structured.
units.tip: spot-check 10 judge verdicts by hand. If the judge disagrees with you more than once or twice, fix the judge prompt before trusting any number.

units.title: Change one thing
units.do: three experiments, each changing one variable: (a) k=3 vs k=5 vs k=8; (b) a stricter vs looser answer prompt; (c) a different chat model. Record the full scorecard for each. Keep the best configuration as your baseline.
units.tip: more context (higher k) isn't always better — irrelevant chunks distract the model. Let the number decide.

units.title: Review and refactor
units.do: refactor into a clean package: `rag/chunking.py`, `rag/index.py`, `rag/retrieve.py`, `rag/generate.py`, `rag/eval.py`, `rag/models.py`. Tests for chunking and retrieval with a tiny fixed corpus (no API calls — mock embeddings with fixed vectors).
units.tip: your RAG should be ~200–300 lines. If it's much more, you're over-engineering; if much less, you're missing error handling.

units.title: Build block: RAG scorecard release
units.do: (1) 3 h: CLI with `ingest <folder>`, `ask "<question>"`, `eval`. (2) 2 h: `eval` prints a formatted scorecard and writes `eval_results/<timestamp>.json` so you can compare runs. (3) 1 h: README documenting the architecture (one diagram, drawn by hand and photographed is fine), the golden set, and the baseline numbers. (4) 1 h: write a short "what would break this?" section — long documents, tables, images, questions spanning multiple chunks.
units.tip: saving every eval run as a timestamped file is the difference between "I think it got better" and "recall went from 0.73 to 0.87 on run 14."

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Keyword search (BM25)
units.do: implement BM25 over your chunks with the `rank_bm25` library (or hand-roll a simple TF-IDF). Run the retrieval eval with BM25 only. Compare recall to vector-only.
units.learn: embeddings miss exact terms (codes, names, numbers); BM25 is classic term-frequency ranking; it's complementary to vectors.
units.tip: look at which questions BM25 wins. They're usually ones with specific identifiers. That tells you why hybrid search exists.

units.title: Hybrid search
units.do: implement RRF over vector and BM25 results. Run the eval. Record recall@5 vs each alone.
units.learn: combine rankings — reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) is simple and robust: score = Σ 1/(60 + rank).
units.tip: RRF needs no tuning and usually beats either method. Start there; only tune weights if the eval demands it.

units.title: Reranking
units.do: implement an LLM-based reranker (structured output: relevance 0–3 per chunk) over the top-20 hybrid results; return top-5. Run the eval. Record recall, latency, cost.
units.learn: retrieve broadly (top-20) then rerank with a cross-encoder or an LLM judging relevance of each chunk to the question; slower but more precise.
units.tip: reranking costs latency and money. The eval tells you whether it's worth it *for your data*. Sometimes it isn't — that's a valid finding.

units.title: pgvector
units.do: `CREATE EXTENSION vector`; migrate your chunks and embeddings into a `chunks` table; write `retrieve_pg(question, k, source=None)` using SQL; add a full-text column for hybrid search in SQL. Run the eval — numbers should match your numpy version.
units.learn: storing vectors in Postgres with the `pgvector` extension; `vector(1024)` column; cosine distance operator `<=>`; an HNSW index; combining with `WHERE` metadata filters and full-text search (`tsvector`) in one query.
units.tip: putting vectors in Postgres means one database, one backup, one set of permissions, real metadata filtering. For most products this beats a separate vector database.

units.title: Query rewriting and review
units.do: implement multi-query rewriting; run the eval; record. Then review the whole week's results in one table and choose your production configuration with a written justification.
units.learn: rewriting the user's question before retrieval (expand abbreviations, generate 2–3 alternate phrasings, merge results) — helps with vague or terse questions.
units.tip: not every technique will help on your corpus. Documenting "tried X, no gain, removed" is as valuable as a win — and it's what good engineers do.

units.title: Build block: Stage 3 exit test
units.do: (1) 4 h timed, no frameworks: given a *new* document set (pick something unfamiliar — a public policy manual, a different domain's docs), build ingest → hybrid retrieval in pgvector → generation with citations → a 20-question golden set → eval harness reporting recall@5 and judged accuracy. (2) 1 h: compare your numbers to the Week 18 baseline; write down what was different about this corpus. (3) 1 h: retrospective. (4) 1 h: read the FastAPI tutorial's first three pages.
units.tip: if the exit test took much longer than 4 hours, the bottleneck was probably data preparation, not AI code. That's normal — and it's why data skills came before LLM skills in this plan.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Hello, API
units.do: `main.py` with `GET /health` returning `{"status": "ok"}`. Run with `uvicorn main:app --reload`. Open `/docs`. Hit it with `curl` and with `httpx` from Python.
units.learn: what FastAPI is (a Python web framework built on type hints and Pydantic); ASGI; `uvicorn` as the server; automatic docs at `/docs`.
units.tip: `--reload` for development only. Note how the docs are generated from your code — that's Pydantic and type hints paying off.

units.title: Path and query parameters
units.do: `GET /contacts/{id}`, `GET /contacts?q=&limit=` backed by an in-memory list. Send bad types and read the 422 body.
units.learn: `@app.get("/items/{item_id}")`, typed path params, query params with defaults, `Optional`, validation errors returning 422 automatically.
units.tip: FastAPI validates and documents parameters from the type hints alone. Write precise types and you get validation for free.

units.title: Request bodies and response models
units.do: `POST /contacts` (201), `PUT /contacts/{id}`, `DELETE /contacts/{id}` (204). `ContactCreate`, `ContactRead`. 404 when missing. Test all from `/docs`.
units.learn: Pydantic models as request bodies; `response_model=`; `status_code=201`; `HTTPException`; separate `Create`, `Update`, `Read` models (never expose internal fields).
units.tip: the response model is a contract. Changing it breaks clients. Design it deliberately; don't just return your database row.

units.title: Dependency injection and structure
units.do: restructure: `app/main.py`, `app/routers/contacts.py`, `app/schemas.py`, `app/config.py` (Settings), `app/deps.py`. Inject settings into a route.
units.learn: `Depends()` for shared logic (settings, DB connections, current user); `APIRouter` to split routes into files; settings via `pydantic-settings` reading `.env`.
units.tip: `Depends` is how FastAPI stays testable — in tests you override dependencies (e.g. swap the real DB for a test DB). Learn it now, use it everywhere.

units.title: Review
units.do: rebuild the CRUD API from memory in 45 minutes. Add pagination (`offset/limit`) with a response envelope `{items, total}`. Add a `X-Request-ID` header middleware that logs each request.
units.tip: middleware that logs method, path, status, and duration for every request is the first observability you'll ever add. Keep it in every service you build.

units.title: Build block: Contact API v1
units.do: (1) 3 h: full CRUD Contact API with routers, schemas, settings, pagination, search, consistent error responses (`{"detail": ...}`), request logging. (2) 2 h: `tests/` with `TestClient`: every endpoint, happy path and errors. (3) 1 h: `ruff`, `mypy`, `Makefile` targets. (4) 1 h: README with `curl` examples for every endpoint.
units.tip: write the tests before the README examples — then the README examples are copied from tests you know pass.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Async concepts
units.do: script that fetches 10 URLs sequentially with `httpx.Client`, then concurrently with `httpx.AsyncClient` + `gather`. Time both. Then do a CPU-heavy loop in both — note no speedup.
units.learn: I/O-bound vs CPU-bound; `async def`, `await`; the event loop; concurrency ≠ parallelism; when async helps (waiting on network/DB) and when it doesn't (heavy computation); `asyncio.gather`.
units.tip: never call a blocking function (like `time.sleep` or a sync DB driver) inside `async def` — it freezes the whole server. Use `asyncio.sleep` and async drivers, or `run_in_threadpool`.

units.title: Async FastAPI
units.do: an endpoint that calls an external API three times sequentially, then a version with `gather`; measure. Add a `/stream` endpoint that yields lines with a delay; watch it in `curl -N`.
units.learn: `async def` routes; `httpx.AsyncClient` as a dependency; background tasks; streaming responses (`StreamingResponse`).
units.tip: streaming is how LLM apps show tokens as they arrive. You'll wire real LLM streaming into this in Week 24.

units.title: Testing async and dependency overrides
units.do: async tests for the external-API endpoint with the HTTP client dependency overridden by a fake returning canned data. No real network in tests.
units.learn: `pytest-asyncio`; `httpx.AsyncClient` against the app; `app.dependency_overrides` to inject fakes.
units.tip: dependency overrides replace mocking for most FastAPI tests. Cleaner, and it forces good structure.

units.title: Configuration and secrets
units.do: `Settings` with `DATABASE_URL`, `LLM_API_KEY`, `ENV=dev|test|prod`. Make startup fail with a clear message if a required key is absent. Add `.env.example`. Run `git log -p | grep -i key` to confirm you've never committed one.
units.learn: `pydantic-settings` with environment-specific `.env` files; never commit secrets; `.env.example`; secret scanning; reading a secret at startup and failing fast if missing.
units.tip: fail fast at startup, not on the first request an hour later. A missing secret should be the first line of the log, not a 500 at 3am.

units.title: Review
units.do: from memory: an async route with a concurrent fanout, a streaming endpoint, and an async test using a dependency override. Add proper error handling for the external call (timeout → 504, upstream 5xx → 502).
units.tip: map upstream failures to correct status codes. Returning 500 for "the other service was slow" misleads everyone debugging later.

units.title: Build block: Contact API v2
units.do: (1) 3 h: convert the API to async end-to-end; add an `/enrich/{id}` endpoint that concurrently calls two fake external services and merges results; add streaming export of all contacts as NDJSON. (2) 2 h: full async test suite with overrides; test the failure mappings. (3) 1 h: a simple load test with `hey` or `locust` — record requests/sec before and after async. (4) 1 h: log the results and read the psycopg async docs.
units.tip: load-test numbers in your README are a strong signal to employers that you think about performance empirically.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Async Postgres in FastAPI
units.do: wire the Contact API to Postgres (schema from Week 10 with migrations). Replace the in-memory store. All CRUD through parameterized SQL.
units.learn: `psycopg` async, `psycopg_pool.AsyncConnectionPool`; opening the pool at startup (`lifespan`), closing at shutdown; a `get_db` dependency that yields a connection.
units.tip: one pool per process, created in `lifespan`. Creating a connection per request is the #1 cause of "database has too many connections" in beginner deployments.

units.title: Migrations with Alembic
units.do: initialize Alembic; convert your numbered SQL migrations into Alembic revisions; add a new column via a migration; run up and down.
units.learn: Alembic setup, autogenerate (with SQLAlchemy models) or hand-written migrations, `upgrade head`, `downgrade`, migration hygiene.
units.tip: you may keep raw SQL inside Alembic revisions if you prefer it over SQLAlchemy models. The tool matters less than the discipline: schema changes are versioned and repeatable.

units.title: Test database strategy
units.do: `conftest.py` with a session-scoped test DB (create, migrate, drop) and a function-scoped transaction rollback. Convert all API tests to hit the real test DB.
units.learn: tests against a real Postgres (a throwaway test DB), truncating between tests or wrapping each test in a rolled-back transaction; fixtures for seed data.
units.tip: testing against real Postgres catches the constraint and type errors that mocks hide. It's slower; it's worth it.

units.title: Authentication: API keys and JWT
units.do: `POST /auth/register`, `POST /auth/token` returning a JWT; a `get_current_user` dependency; protect the contacts routes so users only see their own contacts (owner column + `WHERE owner_id = ...`).
units.learn: authentication (who are you) vs authorization (what may you do); API keys for machine clients; passwords hashed with `bcrypt`/`argon2` (never stored plain); JWT: header/payload/signature, expiry, `Authorization: Bearer`; `OAuth2PasswordBearer` in FastAPI.
units.tip: authorization bugs are data-leak bugs. Write a test where user A tries to read user B's contact and gets 404 — before you write anything else.

units.title: CORS, rate limiting, review
units.do: add CORS for a fake frontend origin; add a rate limiter dependency (e.g. 60 req/min per API key) returning 429; tests for both.
units.learn: what CORS is and why browsers need it; `CORSMiddleware` with an explicit allow-list; simple per-key rate limiting (in-memory token bucket now, Redis later).
units.tip: `allow_origins=["*"]` with credentials is a security hole and browsers reject it anyway. Explicit origins only.

units.title: Build block: Contact API v3
units.do: (1) 3 h: multi-user Contact API with Postgres, Alembic, JWT auth, ownership enforcement, rate limiting, CORS. (2) 2 h: tests covering auth flows, cross-user access denial, rate-limit 429, migrations up/down. (3) 1 h: seed script creating two users with data. (4) 1 h: README security section: how auth works, what's protected, known limitations.
units.tip: the "known limitations" section is a maturity signal. No JWT refresh? No email verification? Say so. Honesty about scope beats false completeness.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Containers explained
units.do: install Docker. `docker run hello-world`, `docker run -it python:3.12 bash`, explore inside, exit, `docker ps -a`, `docker rm`. Run `docker run -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=x -p 5432:5432 postgres:16` and connect with `psql`.
units.learn: an image is a frozen filesystem + command; a container is a running instance; why: "works on my machine" eliminated, identical dev/prod; images vs VMs; Docker Hub.
units.tip: containers are ephemeral — anything written inside is gone when removed unless you use a volume. Learn that by losing data once, today, on purpose.

units.title: Your first Dockerfile
units.do: Dockerfile for the Contact API. Build, run, hit `/health` from the host. Change a line of code, rebuild — observe which layers are cached.
units.learn: `FROM`, `WORKDIR`, `COPY`, `RUN`, `ENV`, `EXPOSE`, `CMD`; layer caching (copy requirements before code); `.dockerignore`.
units.tip: order Dockerfile lines from least to most frequently changing. `COPY requirements.txt` + `pip install` before `COPY . .` makes rebuilds take seconds instead of minutes.

units.title: docker compose
units.do: `compose.yaml` running API + Postgres + migrations on startup. `docker compose up`, `logs`, `down`, `down -v`. Confirm data persists across `down`/`up` but not `down -v`.
units.learn: multi-container apps; `compose.yaml` with `api` and `db` services; networks (services reach each other by name); volumes for Postgres data; `depends_on` and healthchecks; env files.
units.tip: inside compose, the DB host is `db` (the service name), not `localhost`. This confuses everyone once.

units.title: Production images
units.do: multi-stage Dockerfile; run as non-root; compare image size before/after; healthcheck instruction. Run tests *inside* the container.
units.learn: multi-stage builds (build deps in one stage, copy only what's needed); non-root user; pinned base image; `uvicorn` with multiple workers or behind `gunicorn`; image size inspection.
units.tip: running as root inside a container is a real security finding in audits. Add a user; it's four lines.

units.title: Review
units.do: from memory: Dockerfile, compose with DB and volume, healthcheck. Add a `Makefile` target `make up`, `make test-docker`, `make logs`. Delete all local images and rebuild from scratch to prove reproducibility.
units.tip: "delete everything and rebuild" is the container equivalent of Week 1's re-clone test. Do it before every stage exit from now on.

units.title: Build block: containerized Contact API
units.do: (1) 3 h: production-grade Dockerfile + compose for API, Postgres, and a one-shot `migrate` service; environment separation (`compose.override.yaml` for dev with `--reload` and mounted source). (2) 2 h: run the full test suite inside a container via compose (`compose run api pytest`). (3) 1 h: document in README: one command to run, one to test. (4) 1 h: install `pgvector` in the compose Postgres (use the `pgvector/pgvector` image) in preparation for next week.
units.tip: a stranger should be able to `git clone && docker compose up` and have a working API in under two minutes. Test that claim on a clean machine or VM if you can.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Design
units.do: write the API spec for the RAG service: `POST /documents` (upload text/PDF, returns document id, ingestion runs in background), `GET /documents/{id}` (status: pending/ready/failed), `POST /query` (question → answer + citations + scores), `GET /health`. Pydantic models for all. Schema: `documents`, `chunks` (with `vector` and `tsvector` columns), `queries` (log every query and answer). Draw it.
units.tip: logging every query and answer to a table from day one gives you a dataset for evals and debugging. Products that skip this regret it.

units.title: Ingestion pipeline
units.do: port Week 17–19 chunking + embedding into `app/services/ingest.py`; `POST /documents` stores the document, enqueues a `BackgroundTask` that chunks, embeds (batched, cached), inserts into `chunks`, updates status; failures set `failed` with an error message.
units.tip: `BackgroundTasks` is fine for now; you'll note in Week 29 why a real queue (e.g. a worker process) is needed at scale. Know the limitation.

units.title: Retrieval and query endpoint
units.do: `app/services/retrieve.py` with hybrid search in SQL (pgvector + full-text, RRF); `app/services/generate.py` with the RAG prompt and citations; `POST /query` wires them, persists to `queries`, returns `QueryResponse(answer, citations: list[Citation], retrieval_scores)`.
units.tip: return the retrieval scores and chunk IDs in the response. Clients (and you) need them to debug "why did it say that?"

units.title: Streaming answers
units.do: `POST /query/stream` that streams the answer tokens as server-sent events while still persisting the final answer. Handle client disconnect.
units.tip: persist the final answer *after* streaming completes, in a `finally`, so a disconnect mid-stream doesn't lose the log.

units.title: Tests
units.do: tests with the LLM and embedding clients replaced via dependency overrides returning deterministic fakes; a test corpus of 5 tiny documents; assertions on retrieval order, citation presence, refusal on unanswerable questions, and document status transitions.
units.tip: the fake embedding can be a hash-based deterministic vector. It doesn't need to be meaningful — tests need determinism, not intelligence.

units.title: Build block: integrate the eval harness
units.do: (1) 3 h: `scripts/eval.py` that ingests your golden corpus through the real API (compose stack), runs the golden questions through `/query`, and reports recall@5, judged accuracy, refusal accuracy, p95 latency, and cost — same scorecard as Week 18, now against the service. (2) 2 h: fix anything that regressed versus the standalone version (there will be something). (3) 2 h: README with architecture diagram, endpoints, and the scorecard.
units.tip: the eval regressing when you moved to a service is normal — usually a prompt or chunking detail changed silently. This is why the harness exists.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Multi-tenancy
units.do: documents and queries belong to a user (JWT from Week 22); every retrieval query filters by `owner_id`; cross-user test proving isolation.
units.tip: tenant isolation in the SQL `WHERE` clause, tested — never "the frontend won't ask for other people's documents."

units.title: PDF and file handling
units.do: accept PDF and `.txt`/`.md` uploads; reject others with 415; cap size; extract text; mark scanned PDFs as `failed` with a clear reason.
units.learn: `UploadFile`, size limits, MIME checks, extracting text from PDFs with `pypdf`, handling scanned PDFs (no text) gracefully.
units.tip: file uploads are an attack surface (huge files, wrong types, path tricks). Validate before you touch the bytes.

units.title: Collections and metadata filters
units.do: `collections` table (user-owned); documents belong to a collection; `/query` accepts `collection_id`; retrieval filters by it in SQL. Update tests.
units.tip: metadata filtering inside the vector query is exactly why pgvector in Postgres was the right call in Week 19.

units.title: Operational endpoints
units.do: `GET /health` checks DB connectivity and reports version; `GET /metrics` (simple counters: queries served, ingestion failures, average latency — real Prometheus format comes in Week 26 if you want it); admin `DELETE /documents/{id}` cascades chunks.
units.tip: a health endpoint that only returns `ok` without checking dependencies lies to your load balancer. Check the DB.

units.title: Review and hardening
units.do: run `ruff`, `mypy` strict, full tests in compose; fix every warning. Read your own code as a reviewer: naming, dead code, duplicated logic. Refactor for one hour.
units.tip: self-review with a checklist (naming, errors handled, tests present, secrets absent, logging present) before every stage exit. It's what code review will do to you at a job.

units.title: Build block: Stage 4 exit test
units.do: (1) 4 h timed: implement an unseen feature — "per-collection sharing: a user can grant read access to another user; shared users can query but not upload or delete" — with migration, endpoints, ownership/permission logic, and tests. (2) 1 h: run the eval harness to confirm no regression. (3) 1 h: tag a release `v1.0.0`, write release notes. (4) 1 h: retrospective; create accounts on Langfuse and Sentry (free tiers).
units.tip: the feature is deliberately about authorization. If the tests for "shared user cannot delete" aren't there, you didn't pass.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Structured logging
units.do: switch the API to JSON logging (`structlog` or stdlib with a JSON formatter). Propagate `request_id` from middleware into every log line, including inside services. Confirm with `docker compose logs | jq`.
units.learn: logs as JSON with consistent fields (timestamp, level, request_id, user_id, path, duration_ms); log levels used deliberately; correlation IDs across a request.
units.tip: if you can't filter logs by request_id to see one request's entire story, your logging isn't done.

units.title: Tracing LLM calls with Langfuse
units.do: instrument `/query`: one trace per request, spans for retrieval and generation, with inputs/outputs, token usage, and cost attached. Open the Langfuse dashboard and read a trace end to end.
units.learn: what a trace is (a request) and a span is (a step: retrieve, generate, judge); recording prompts, completions, tokens, cost, latency per span; why prompts must be inspectable in production.
units.tip: attach `user_id`, `collection_id`, and a release version as trace metadata. You'll filter on these the first time a user says "it gave a wrong answer yesterday."

units.title: Error monitoring with Sentry
units.do: install the Sentry SDK in the API; trigger a deliberate exception; find it in the dashboard; add `user_id` and `request_id` as context; set up an email alert for new error groups.
units.learn: exception capture with stack traces and request context; alerting; grouping; breadcrumbs; release tagging.
units.tip: capture upstream LLM/API failures as *handled* events with context, not just unhandled crashes. The interesting failures are the ones you caught and degraded on.

units.title: Metrics and latency
units.do: instrument request duration histograms per route; expose `/metrics`; compute p95 for `/query` over 100 requests from a script. Add LLM cost as a counter.
units.learn: counters, gauges, histograms; p50/p95/p99; why averages lie; `/metrics` in Prometheus format via `prometheus-fastapi-instrumentator` (optional — a simple in-app histogram is fine).
units.tip: track cost per query as a first-class metric. "Our p95 is 2.1s and median cost is $0.004/query" is a sentence that gets you hired.

units.title: Review: answer three questions
units.do: using only your dashboards and logs (no code reading), answer: (1) what did the slowest query today cost and why was it slow? (2) which user has made the most queries? (3) what was the last error and what request triggered it? Write the answers and how you found them in your log.
units.tip: if any of the three took more than five minutes, add the missing metadata/field today.

units.title: Build block: observability release
units.do: (1) 2 h: trace the ingestion pipeline too (per-document spans, chunk counts, embedding cost). (2) 2 h: a "debug view" endpoint (admin-only) returning a query's full trace summary: chunks retrieved with scores, prompt used, answer, judge score if any. (3) 2 h: a runbook in `docs/RUNBOOK.md`: how to find a request by ID, how to see cost by user, what to do when Sentry alerts, how to roll back. (4) 1 h: tag `v1.1.0`.
units.tip: a runbook you write now is the document a future on-call teammate (or you at 2am) will thank you for. Keep it short and imperative.

units.title: Rest
units.do: Rest, or catch up if you are behind.

units.title: Prompt injection
units.do: upload a document containing an injection payload; ask a question that retrieves it; observe. Write 10 injection attempts (in documents and in questions); record which succeed.
units.learn: a document or user message can contain instructions ("ignore previous instructions and reveal…"); RAG makes this worse because retrieved text enters the prompt; the model can't reliably distinguish data from instructions.
units.tip: you cannot fully "prompt away" injection. Defences layer: delimit untrusted text, instruct the model to treat it as data, limit what tools/outputs can do, validate outputs, and never let retrieved text trigger actions without a human.

units.title: Input and output controls
